notes.b: Geographers group places into regions by how wealthy and developed they are, not just by landscape. A socio-economic region is defined by its level of wealth and development, judged by several indicators at once, because no single figure tells the whole story.
points: The indicators include income or GDP per head (the value of what an area produces, divided by its population), unemployment, the mix of primary, secondary and tertiary jobs, migration, age structure, education and services.

Primary jobs take materials from the land and sea (farming, fishing, forestry, mining); secondary jobs make goods in factories; tertiary jobs provide services. The mix of these three is a clue to how developed a region is.

The core–periphery idea: wealth, people and investment (money put into businesses and infrastructure) concentrate in a core, while the periphery (the outer, distant area) loses people and capital to it.
Cumulative causation means each advantage in the core attracts more, so the gap tends to widen unless governments or the EU intervene.
notes.tip: Describe a region using several indicators together, not one, as the definition itself says.

notes.b: A core region has a strong, growing economy, high incomes, and a concentration of population, investment and decision-making. Everything else about it follows from that economic strength.
points: It has high GDP per head and low unemployment, because jobs are plentiful.
It has a large tertiary (services) sector, including finance, company headquarters and high-tech industry.
Most foreign investment goes to the core, because firms from abroad want its markets, workers and transport links.
Net in-migration (more people arriving than leaving) of young, educated workers gives it a young population, because they move to where the jobs are.
It has dense, well-developed infrastructure (the transport networks that move people and goods): motorways, airports, ports and rail lines.
It has universities and research institutions, which supply skilled workers, and usually the capital city with the seat of government.

Causes: accessibility, a large market and labour force, an early start, government and capital functions, and agglomeration, where firms attract more firms to the same place because they gain from being near suppliers, customers and workers.
Problems of success: congestion, high house prices, urban sprawl (the city spreading outwards over farmland) and pressure on services.
notes.tip: Core regions have net in-migration, not out-migration, and they attract industry. If asked to name a core region and explain why it is core, give the region and then several of its characteristics.

notes.b: Three examples show what a core looks like at national and European scale. Each is a place where population, government and business cluster.
points: Greater Dublin Area: Dublin, Kildare, Meath and Wicklow. County Dublin had about 1.45 million people in Census 2022, when the State's population was about 5.1 million.

Dublin, the capital, has the seat of government, Ireland's main port (Dublin Port) and busiest airport (Dublin Airport). Its docklands host the European headquarters of many technology firms, e.g. Google. There is more on this in the Irish Regions chapter.
Paris Basin, France: Île-de-France, the region around Paris at the basin's core, has about 12 million people. There is more on this in the European Regions chapter.

The Blue Banana: the curved belt of Europe's main core, running from south-east England and London through the Benelux countries (Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg) and the Rhine valley to northern Italy (Milan).
notes.tip: The Paris Basin and the Greater Dublin Area are the core regions exams match. The Paris Basin is a core region, not a region of industrial decline. Give County Dublin and State figures only, not totals for the whole Greater Dublin Area.

notes.b: A peripheral region is distant, physically or economically, from the core, with a weaker economy and fewer opportunities. Its problems tend to feed each other, so people leave and the region falls further behind.
points: Remote location and poor access to markets and services, so it is costly to sell goods or reach shops, hospitals and schools.
Difficult physical conditions: mountains, high rainfall, poor soils and a short growing season, which limit what farmers can produce.
Dependence on primary activity (taking materials from land and sea): small farms, fishing and forestry.
Low incomes and higher unemployment, so people look elsewhere for work, or underemployment (people working fewer hours or in lower-skilled jobs than they want).
Net out-migration of young adults, so the people left behind are older and rural populations fall.
Fewer services, and small, scattered settlements, which means services costly to provide.
notes.tip: Peripheral regions have net out-migration, and a peripheral region is the opposite of a core. Be ready to give the definition of a peripheral region.

notes.b: Because the periphery tends to fall further behind, governments and the EU act to slow the loss of people and jobs.
points: EU regional and cohesion funds (money meant to narrow the gap between richer and poorer regions) and state agencies channel investment into the periphery.
Better roads and broadband, and decentralisation of government offices (moving them out of the capital), help peripheral areas keep people and jobs.
Tourism builds on the scenery and culture of peripheral areas, so it brings jobs without needing a nearby core.
There is more on each example in the case-study chapters.

notes.b: These four examples are far from their country's or Europe's core, in the west, south and far north.
points: West of Ireland: the Northern and Western regional assembly area. Co. Leitrim has the smallest population of any Irish county.
The Mezzogiorno, southern Italy. There is more on this in the European Regions chapter.
Northern Norway: Arctic, remote and reliant on fishing.
North-west Scotland: the Highlands and Islands.
notes.tip: Exams match the West of Ireland, the BMW region, the Mezzogiorno and northern Norway as peripheral regions. For a 30-mark question, name one and explain why it is peripheral, using the characteristics above.

notes.b: A less-developed region is defined by how far its development falls below an average, and the EU uses a precise cut-off to decide which regions get the most help.
points: A less-developed region is one whose level of development is well below the national or EU average.
In EU regional policy, a less-developed region has GDP per head below 75% of the EU average, and receives the most EU aid.
Most less-developed regions in Europe are also peripheral: the Mezzogiorno, and much of eastern Europe such as Romania and Bulgaria.
Peripheral is not the same as less-developed, because a peripheral region can lie in a rich country, such as the West of Ireland or northern Norway.
Ireland was a single Objective 1 region (the category receiving the highest level of EU aid) until 1999. From 2000 to 2006 only the BMW (Border, Midland and Western) region kept Objective 1 status.
At a global scale, less-developed regions are developing countries. India is the continental example. There is more on India in its own chapter.
The Mezzogiorno's development history began with the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno (Fund for the South) in 1950.
notes.tip: Keep peripheral and less-developed apart: a region can be peripheral inside a rich country, as the West of Ireland and northern Norway are. Make the distinction in one clear sentence.

notes.b: A region of industrial decline grew on heavy, traditional industry and has since lost much of it. The loss then spreads through the local economy.
points: Its traditional industries include coal mining, iron and steel, shipbuilding and textiles.

Causes: coal seams exhausted or too costly to work; cheaper imports and competition from newly industrialised countries (countries that built up their factory industry more recently, often with lower costs).
Further causes: coal replaced by oil and gas; out-of-date plant (old machinery and factories); and automation (machines doing work people once did), which needs fewer workers.
Effects: high unemployment, especially among older male workers; derelict factories, mines and spoil heaps (waste rock dumped from mining); and polluted land.
Further effects: out-migration, falling services, and a poor image that deters new investment.

Responses: retraining; clearing and cleaning derelict land; attracting new light industry and services; universities and technology parks; reuse of industrial heritage for tourism and culture; EU funds.
notes.tip: High unemployment and abandoned factories mark regions of industrial decline. These regions lost their industry, so do not call the Ruhr a core region.

notes.b: Most examples are old coal and steel regions of north-west Europe. The Irish examples are port and shipbuilding areas.
points: Sambre–Meuse valley, Wallonia, Belgium: coal mining and steel along the Sambre and Meuse, e.g. Charleroi on the Sambre and Liège on the Meuse.
Ruhr, Germany (North Rhine-Westphalia): Europe's largest coal and steel region, so its decline was large, with cities such as Essen, Dortmund and Duisburg.

Prosper-Haniel in Bottrop, the last hard-coal mine in Germany, closed in 2018. The Zollverein coal mine complex in Essen became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001 and is now a cultural centre, an example of reusing industrial heritage.
South Wales coalfield, including the Rhondda valleys: coal mining collapsed in the late 20th century.
Nord–Pas-de-Calais, France, is a further European example.
Belfast, for example: the Harland and Wolff shipyard, which built the Titanic (launched 1911), declined greatly in the late 20th century.

Dublin docklands: port jobs fell with containerisation (goods shipped in standard metal containers, which need far fewer dock workers). The International Financial Services Centre (IFSC), established in 1987 on derelict dockland, regenerated the area.
There is more on Irish economic evidence in the Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Economic Activities chapter.
notes.tip: Exams match the Sambre–Meuse valley, the Ruhr and the South Wales coalfields as regions of industrial decline.

notes.b: The clearest difference between the two region types is the kind of work people do. Compare them sector by sector: primary, secondary and tertiary.
points: Primary, for example: large, commercial, efficient farms on good land in the core; small, fragmented farms on poor land in the periphery, with more fishing and forestry.

Secondary: concentrations of manufacturing and multinational investment (factories owned by firms based in other countries) in the core; few, small and often grant-aided (helped by state money) factories in the periphery.
Tertiary: finance, headquarters, government, universities, and major ports and airports in the core; tourism and public services in the periphery.
notes.tip: Higher Level exams set a 30-mark question on how economic activity in core regions differs from that in peripheral regions. Answer in paired points, core against periphery, for each of the three sectors.

keyTerms.definition: A region defined by its level of wealth and development, judged by several indicators together.
A region with a strong, growing economy and a concentration of population, investment and decision-making.
A region distant, physically or economically, from the core, with a weaker economy and fewer opportunities.
The process by which advantages in a core attract further growth, widening the gap with the periphery.
A region whose development is well below the national or EU average; in EU policy, GDP per head below 75% of the EU average.
A region that grew on heavy, traditional industry and has since lost much of it.
The clustering of firms in one place, which attracts more firms because of shared markets, labour and services.

questions.prompt: Contrast the primary, secondary and tertiary activities of a core region and a peripheral region you have studied.
questions.model: Primary: core regions have large, commercial, efficient farms on good land, while the West of Ireland periphery has small, fragmented farms on poor land, with more fishing and forestry. Secondary: the core attracts manufacturing and multinational investment, while the periphery has few, small and often grant-aided factories. Tertiary: the core has finance, company headquarters, government, universities, and major ports and airports, while the periphery depends on tourism and public services. Causes: the core's accessibility, large market and labour force, and agglomeration draw investment in; the periphery's remoteness, difficult physical conditions and out-migration of young adults keep it weak. Effects: the core has congestion, high house prices and urban sprawl, while the periphery has an ageing population, falling rural numbers and fewer services. Responses in the periphery include EU regional and cohesion funds, better roads and broadband, and tourism.

questions.prompt: Examine the causes and effects of industrial decline in a region you have studied.
questions.model: Example: the Ruhr in western Germany. It was Europe's largest coal and steel region, with cities including Essen, Dortmund and Duisburg. Causes: coal seams became exhausted or too costly to work; cheaper imports and competition from newly industrialised countries; coal was replaced by oil and gas; plant was out of date; and automation needed fewer workers. Effects: high unemployment, especially among older male workers; derelict factories, mines and spoil heaps; polluted land; out-migration; falling services; and a poor image that deters new investment. Responses: the last hard-coal mine, Prosper-Haniel in Bottrop, closed in 2018; the Zollverein coal mine complex in Essen, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001, was converted into a cultural centre; derelict land was cleared and cleaned; new light industry, services, universities and technology parks were attracted; and EU funds supported retraining and renewal.

questions.prompt: Describe the main characteristics of (i) a core region and (ii) a peripheral region, naming an example of each.
questions.model: (i) Core region: strong, growing economy with high GDP per head and low unemployment; a large tertiary sector with finance, headquarters and high-tech industry; most foreign investment; net in-migration of young, educated workers; dense infrastructure of motorways, airports, ports and rail; universities; and usually the capital city. Example: the Greater Dublin Area (Dublin, Kildare, Meath and Wicklow), with County Dublin home to about 1.45 million people in Census 2022. (ii) Peripheral region: distant from the core with poor access; difficult physical conditions such as mountains, high rainfall and poor soils; dependence on small farms, fishing and forestry; low incomes and higher unemployment; net out-migration of young adults and an ageing population; fewer services and small, scattered settlements. Example: the West of Ireland, the Northern and Western regional assembly area.
